title: Connections: the maximum, and why raising it is rarely the fix

videos.script: Every connection to PostgreSQL is a process. {{ps}} Not a thread, and not a row in a table. It is a whole operating-system process, started by the postmaster when a client knocks and gone when the client leaves. {{limit}} That is why there is a maximum, and why the maximum is small. The default is a hundred. {{fatal}} In this lesson you lower it to five and run into it for real. You will see the two refusals PostgreSQL gives. You will also see the three slots it keeps back for a superuser, which only help if the application is not one. {{raise}} The usual reaction to too many clients is to raise the number. So you raise it, and measure what that costs. Shared memory grows before anybody connects. And on a machine with four processors, eighty clients get no more done than four, each of them waiting far longer. {{idle}} Often the real problem is a connection doing nothing while it holds a transaction open. You will find one, end it, and set a timeout so the server ends the next one by itself. {{pool}} And you will see why the lasting answer is usually a pooler, which two later courses teach. {{title}}
